content: Brivaracetam is a third-generation antiepileptic drug that acts as a high-affinity ligand for synaptic vesicle protein 2A. It is used as an add-on therapy for individuals with drug-resistant epilepsy, a condition where up to 30% of patients continue to experience seizures despite treatment with antiepileptic drugs. These patients often require a combination of multiple antiepileptic medications. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of brivaracetam as an add-on treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy. The latest update involved a search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Register of Studies, MEDLINE, and others, up to September 2021. The review focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that included participants of any age with drug-resistant epilepsy. Studies with any level of blinding (double-blind, single-blind, or unblinded) were considered. The primary outcome assessed was the proportion of participants achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency. Secondary outcomes included seizure freedom, treatment withdrawal for any reason, treatment withdrawal due to adverse events, the proportion of participants experiencing adverse events, and drug interactions. Data were analyzed using an intention-to-treat approach, and results were presented as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). No new studies were identified for this update, so the results and conclusions remain unchanged from the previous review. The review included six studies with a total of 2,411 participants. Five of these studies focused on individuals with focal-onset seizures, while only one study included participants with both focal and generalized-onset seizures. Participants ranged in age from 16 to 80 years, and treatment periods lasted between 7 and 16 weeks. Two studies were judged to have a low risk of bias, while four had an unclear risk of bias. Some studies lacked sufficient details on allocation concealment and blinding methods. One study failed to report all prespecified outcomes, and another showed discrepancies in reporting. Participants receiving brivaracetam as an add-on therapy were more likely to achieve a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency compared to those receiving placebo (RR 1.81, 95% CI 1.53 to 2.14; moderate-certainty evidence). They were also more likely to achieve seizure freedom, although the evidence for this outcome was of low certainty (RR 5.89, 95% CI 2.30 to 15.13). The incidence of treatment withdrawal for any reason was slightly higher in the brivaracetam group compared to the placebo group (RR 1.27, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.74; low-certainty evidence). The risk of experiencing one or more adverse events was not significantly different between the brivaracetam and placebo groups (RR 1.08, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.17; moderate-certainty evidence). However, participants receiving brivaracetam were more likely to withdraw from treatment due to adverse events (RR 1.54, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.33; low-certainty evidence). In conclusion, brivaracetam may be effective in reducing seizure frequency and helping patients achieve seizure freedom when used as an add-on therapy for drug-resistant epilepsy. However, it is likely associated with a higher rate of treatment withdrawals due to adverse events compared to placebo. It is important to note that only one study included participants with generalized epilepsy, and none of the studies involved individuals under the age of 16. Additionally, all studies were of short duration. Therefore, the findings are primarily applicable to adult patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Future research should focus on the long-term tolerability and efficacy of brivaracetam, as well as its use in other types of seizures and age groups.
